chat.author: Jari Arkko
chat.text: I'm not sure the call and SMS example is giving the right model for the one-or-multiple dialogs discussion. I think we're hitting the same problem as we had in the previous presentation, we're trying to craft concepts whereas the thing we should think about is the real world. In the real world, you want the identities for the call and the SMS destination to be the same, and have some shared context of what should be said on both. But it doesn't follow that we need to share my credit card details with my SMS agent. Can we do share-information-on-a-need-basis instead? Even if the all the conversations in Jonathan's slide are part of the same bigger context, we don't have to share everything to everyone. Just what is is needed for the tasks at hand.

chat.text: @arashmid: I agree with multiple dialogues per activity. But this is boundless in some senses as there are multiple activities per activity etc. There is a complexity where there is a subcontractor (delegation) that was invisible but that then becomes visible  as a result of a need to interact with a party back up the chain (I am thinking of when my builder asked me to sort out a challenge he had with his roofing supplier). I suspect that this is a separate dialogue within some layered collection of activities. The protocol is dealing only with dialogue (I have with the roofing provider and my builder in the context of the roofing). BUT somewhere else that layering of activities is dealt with.

chat.author: Edgar Orendain
chat.text:
FWIW, I like draft-reddy-wimse-oauth-dialog-binding-00's position that:
"At a trust boundary, a participant initiates a linked dialog ... Neither the dialog identifier nor the transaction token of the original domain crosses the boundary."
Makes less assumptions about what trust domain admins may or may not be willing to make available in dialogs escaping that domain.
But I then wonder how we'd do things the use cases draft or charter suggests (e.g., full-chain verifications).
